'''''Pyrus cordata''''', the '''Plymouth pear''',<ref name="PlantAtlas">{{cite web |title=Plymouth Pear ''Pyrus cordata'' Desv. |website=PlantAtlas |url=https://plantatlas2020.org/atlas/2cd4p9h.r57 |access-date=2026-07-13}}</ref> is a rare wild species of [[pear]] belonging to the family [[Rosaceae]]. It gets its scientific name {{lang|la|cordata}} and French names {{lang|fr|Poirier à feuilles en cœur, Poirier à feuilles cordées}} from the shape of its leaves.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Stearn |first1=William T. |title=Botanical Latin |date=1983 |publisher=David & Charles |isbn=0-7153-8548-8 |page=407}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://florelocale.fr/encyclopedie/index.php/Pyrus_cordata|title = ''Pyrus cordata'', Heart leaved pear tree|date = 19 October 2023}}</ref> The English name Plymouth pear is after the city of [[Plymouth]] in [[Devon]], where it was originally found in 1870<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.woodlandtrust.org.uk/visiting-woods/trees-woods-and-wildlife/british-trees/native-trees/plymouth-pear/ |title=Plymouth pear (''Pyrus cordata'') - Woodland Trust |access-date=2016-08-03 |archive-date=2019-02-12 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190212081423/http://www.woodlandtrust.org.uk/visiting-woods/trees-woods-and-wildlife/british-trees/native-trees/plymouth-pear/ }}</ref> The Plymouth pear was one of the British trees to be funded under [[English Nature]]s Species Recovery Programme.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.fwi.co.uk/news/help-preserve-a-tree-with-ancient-british-connection.htm|title = Help preserve a tree with ancient British connection|date = 22 August 1997|work=Farmers Weekly}}</ref>

It is a small tree, that grows in hedgerows or at the edge of woods.
The Plymouth pear is considered to be either a subspecies of [[Pyrus pyraster|''Pyrus pyraster'' (European wild pear)]] or a distinct species.{{citation needed|date=February 2012}} It is one of the rarest trees in the UK and it is protected under Schedule 8 of the [[Wildlife and Countryside Act]] and seeds have been deposited at [[Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew|Kew]]'s [[Millennium Seed Bank]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.woodlandtrust.org.uk/trees-woods-and-wildlife/british-trees/a-z-of-british-trees/plymouth-pear/|title=Plymouth Pear, ''Pyrus cordata''|website=Woodland Trust}}</ref>

==Description==
''Pyrus cordata'' is a deciduous shrub or small tree growing up to {{convert|10|m}} in height.
It is hardy and is not frost tender, but its ability to bear fruit and thus seed is dependent upon favourable weather conditions.
It is in flower from April to May. The flowers are hermaphroditic and are pollinated by insects. The trees have pale cream blossom with some pink.
The smell of the blossom has however been described as a faint but disgusting smell compared to rotting [[scampi]], soiled sheets or wet carpets. The odour attracts mainly flies including some more often drawn to decaying plant matter such as ''[[Bibio marci]]''. It is common in [[Brittany]], Northern [[Portugal]] and [[Galicia (Spain)|Galicia]] where it occurs at woodland margins and scrub on acid soils.{{cn|date=December 2023}}

==Distribution==
The Plymouth pear has an Atlantic distribution and is found in [[Western Europe]] in [[France]] (notably in [[Brittany]]), [[Spain]] (notably in [[Galicia (Spain)|Galicia]]), [[Portugal]] and with a small presence in the [[United Kingdom]] (in [[Devon]] and [[Cornwall]]) where it is now believed to be an [[archaeophyte]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Pyrus cordata Desv. {{!}} Plants of the World Online {{!}} Kew Science |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:730782-1 |website=Plants of the World Online |access-date=21 February 2026 |language=en}}</ref>

==Habitat==
It occurs in thickets, hedgerows, scrub and open woods with cool-temperate climates, in lowlands and hills. Not much about its requirements in the UK are known, but conservationists are looking at how it behaves in [[Brittany]] to get an idea about its requirements.{{cn|date=December 2023}}

===English population===
The species receives its English name from the area it was originally found growing in Plymouth in 1871 by a local naturalist, T. R. Archer Briggs. In the United Kingdom the species is very rare and is confined to two areas – [[Plymouth]] and [[Truro]].
The genetic diversity of the species in the UK is very low with the two widely scattered populations being genetically identical which suggests that one of the populations was established from clonal material taken from the other (suckers or cuttings).<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://www.brc.ac.uk/plantatlas/index.php?q=node/49|series=British Red Data Books|title=1. Vascular plants|edition=3rd|year=1999}}</ref>

However this lack of genetic diversity is a threat to the population because most of the seeds are infertile, but efforts are being made to conserve the population by controlled breeding of trees in botanical gardens and by attempting to induce genetic mutations and variation in cultivated specimens.
Genetic material from other parts of Europe is being avoided, so no trees are being introduced from the mainland European population.
The conservation of the species involves attempting to increase the genetic diversity and so it is hoped that some mutations will take place with the cultivated stock which it is hoped will allow them to breed more successfully (Pears are self-sterile, so clones cannot breed easily with other clones).{{cn|date=December 2023}}

The species suffers from low seed fertility caused by the inbreeding of the two, British populations and conservation efforts are attempting to combat this.
The two populations are also threatened by the use of the landscape but they are being preserved in protected areas in their range.{{cn|date=December 2023}}

Botanists at [[Kew Gardens]] where conservation efforts are taking place have concluded that the Plymouth pear was brought from [[Brittany]] as a hedging plant several hundred years ago.{{cn|date=December 2023}}
